source.title: Scaling-laws for Large Time-series Models
source.citation: Thomas D. P. Edwards et al., 2024
source.authors: Thomas D. P. Edwards; James Alvey; J. Alsing; Nam H. Nguyen; Benjamin Dan Wandelt

record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling behavior in time-series models and refines the simple power-law picture with mild curve breaks, learning-rate sensitivity, and a data-diversity requirement.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling sweeps, architecture and learning-rate sensitivity, and forecasting examples. It cites language-model scaling results as motivation, but those cited results are not recorded as rows. It does not test whether small language-model runs predict much larger language-model runs or the compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own scaling sweeps (parameters, data, compute) on decoder-only time-series transformers and fits power laws to test loss. That is a new modality with a direct result on V5. It also has architecture-sensitivity and roll-out results in that setting (V4, V6) and setup-dependence findings (V7). It mostly confirms the claim rather than arguing against it, so T3 fits better than the reader's T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that decoder-only time-series transformers show LLM-like power-law scaling with parameters, data and compute, spanning up to about five orders of magnitude, and that aspect ratio and head count have minimal effect over broad ranges. They note mild breaks for MSE and CRPS, the need to preserve data diversity for data scaling, the strong dependence on max learning rate, and possible non-convergence of the log-likelihood compute fits.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses scaling sweeps and power-law fits on decoder-only transformers, but studies time-series models rather than language models, uses MSE, CRPS, and log-likelihood rather than held-out cross-entropy, and examines its own corpus and training setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Maximum learning rate varies in importance with model size; aspect ratio affects performance at high values; preserving data diversity is necessary for clear dataset-scaling behavior.
record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2024 Workshop on Time Series in the Age of Large Models
record.problems: The study is limited to univariate time series, a single decoder-only architecture family, and one assembled corpus. MSE and CRPS show mild breaks; compute scaling contains substantial training noise, and log-likelihood may not be fully converged. Forecasting evidence is described through three examples and qualitative figure results; uncertainty estimates are not reported.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out cross-entropy; the study covers only time-series models (MSE, CRPS, Student-t log-likelihood).
No test of whether small-run fits predict much larger runs; post-break fits are only motivated as relevant for extrapolation.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is not studied.
Only aspect ratio and head count, only in time-series models, mostly via CRPS; no language models, and no other architecture details such as d_ff ratio, since d_m = d_ff is fixed.
Image, video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested; only univariate time-series pretraining is covered.
No quantitative downstream metric and no multi-horizon forecasting scaling; only three illustrated roll-outs.
No comparison of published laws, no test of parameter-counting choices, and no test of compute-optimal split sensitivity.

missing.what: Authors note that the constant +2 added to log-likelihood can change the fitted power-law slope. This is a fitting choice that affects the exponent and bears on V7; footnote 2 is text-only.

Exponents differ strongly by metric (e.g. parameter B0 is 0.042 for MSE, 0.036 for CRPS and 0.151 for log-likelihood), so the fitted law depends on the loss used. These values are recorded in rows, but no row frames the comparison.

record.verdict_notes: Workshop paper with a single architecture and one corpus; no uncertainties are reported on the fits. V4, V6 and V7 are linked here in the time-series setting, since those versions do not name a modality; researchers should weigh them as out-of-modality evidence. The training budget is fixed at 10^5 steps for all models, and compute scaling uses the minimum loss envelope over training curves.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling; the study uses time-series models and MSE, CRPS, and log-likelihood instead.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger language-model runs.
The compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its exponents.
The study tests aspect ratio and attention-head count, but not every architectural detail named in the version.
The study tests univariate time-series models, not image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study shows forecasting roll-outs for three datasets, not a broad downstream-task benchmark.
The study does not compare published language-model laws or test parameter-counting choices or compute-optimal allocation fitting choices.

rows.subject: decoder-only time-series transformer models
rows.size_stated: ∼10^3 to ∼10^8 trainable parameters across the scaling runs
rows.operation_detail: Scaled parameter count and fitted a power law to minimum in-sequence test loss.
rows.measure: Minimum in-sequence test MSE; fitted power law after the observed break
rows.value: log10(A0) = -19.47; B0 = 0.042; scaling over nearly five orders of magnitude, with a mild break
rows.locator: Results, Parameter scaling; Fig. 1; Appendix D, Table 7
rows.note: The authors report approximate power-law behavior, but describe a mild break for MSE; the reported fit is after the break.
rows.check: State is relative to V5: a single power law does not hold across the range (mild break for small models), and the fit covers only the post-break part. For V7 the bend counts as observed.

conditions.value: maximum learning rate; dependence examined across parameter counts

rows.locator: Appendix C, Learning-rate and architecture dependence; Fig. 3
rows.note: Text says performance depends on maximum learning rate and that the dependence varies with parameter count; a clear optimum exists, above which models diverge. The optimal maximum learning rate decreases with model size.
rows.check: The text states that LR dependence is strong enough that a smaller model can beat a larger one if the LR is mistuned, and that the optimal LR shrinks with size. So the scaling curve depends on the LR schedule choice. The measure shows setup dependence of performance, not changed exponents directly.

relationships.condition: Univariate time-series decoder-only transformers: log-likelihood parameter and compute scaling, and diversity-preserving data scaling (all metrics)
relationships.reason: Power-law fits hold with little or no break: log-likelihood over about five orders of magnitude in parameters (r3) and in compute (r6), and all three metrics over four orders of magnitude in data (r7, r8, r9).
relationships.display_finding: Log-likelihood power laws held across about five orders of magnitude in parameters and compute, while all three metrics scaled across four orders in diversity-preserving data.

relationships.condition: MSE and CRPS versus parameters and compute; data scaling that does not preserve diversity
relationships.reason: MSE and CRPS show mild breaks for small models and low compute, so the reported fit covers only the post-break part (r1, r2, r4, r5). Without preserved data diversity there was no clear scaling (r10).
relationships.display_finding: MSE and CRPS fits covered only the region after small-model and low-compute breaks, and no clear scaling appeared when data diversity was not preserved.
